title: The Great Tug-of-War: Restrictive vs. Paralytic Strabismus
summary: A definitive clinical guide to differentiating mechanical ocular tethering from innervational failure. Mastery of the Forced Acton Test, saccadic velocities, and orbital imaging is essential for the strabismologist.

sections.title: Clinical Definitions & Core Concepts
sections.content: Restrictive Strabismus results from mechanical tethering or structural interference with the globe's rotation (e.g., fibrosis, entrapment, or orbital masses). Paralytic Strabismus (Paretic) results from a defect in the efferent pathway, including the cranial nerve nuclei, the nerves themselves (CN III, IV, VI), or the neuromuscular junction, leading to muscle weakness.

sections.title: The Deciding Factor: Forced Acton Test (FAT)
content: Step 1: Instill topical anesthetic (Proparacaine 0.5%) and optional 4% Cocaine for vasoconstriction.
Step 2: Grasp the globe at the limbus with toothed forceps (0.5mm Castroviejo) opposite the direction of limited movement.
Step 3: Attempt to move the globe passively into the field of restricted gaze.
Step 4: POSITIVE result = Resistance felt (Restrictive etiology).
Step 5: NEGATIVE result = No resistance (Paralytic/Paretic etiology).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls: Saccades & IOP
content: Saccadic Velocity: In 6th nerve palsy, the eye moves slowly toward abduction. In TED, the eye moves fast until it hits the 'tether'.
IOP Differential: Check IOP in primary position and upgaze. A rise of >4mmHg in upgaze suggests inferior rectus restriction (TED).
Secondary Deviations: In paralytic cases, the deviation is greater when the paretic eye is fixing.
Old Photos: Use the 'Krimsky' version of the 'Shoebox test' (looking at old photos) to determine chronicity.

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Worry
content: Sudden onset painful 3rd nerve palsy (Aneurysm/SAH until proven otherwise).
Bilateral 6th nerve palsy (Raised intracranial pressure).
Variable ptosis and diplopia (Myasthenia Gravis - potential respiratory crisis).
Proptosis with restriction (Orbital Cellulitis or Malignancy).

content.explanation: Order of muscle involvement in Thyroid Eye Disease (most common restrictive): Inferior Rectus > Medial Rectus > Superior Rectus > Lateral Rectus > Obliques.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup: Step-by-Step
content: 1. Motor Exam: 9 positions of gaze, Prism Cover Test (distinguish comitant vs incomitant).
2. Sensory Exam: Worth 4-Dot, Bagolini lenses, Stereoacuity.
3. Forced Acton Test: Essential for confirming mechanical tethering.
4. Laboratory: TSH, TSI (for TED), Acetylcholine receptor antibodies (for MG).
5. Imaging: CT Orbit (axial/coronal) for bone/muscle bulk; MRI for nerves/brainstem.

rows: Large Recessions ONLY. Faden operation (Cüppers). Adjustable sutures recommended.
Resection/Recession (R&R) if some function remains. Transpositions (e.g., Nishida) if total palsy.

sections.title: Surgical Nuance: The 'Golden Rule'
content: NEVER perform a muscle RESECTION in a restrictive disease. It will worsen the restriction.
In complete 6th nerve palsy, a simple recession/resection is useless; a Transposition (e.g., Hummelsheim or Schillinger) is required.
In TED surgery: 'When in doubt, recess more.' Always use adjustable sutures to account for post-operative tissue creep.

sections.title: Landmark Studies: The PEDIG Impact
sections.content: Recent Pediatric Eye Disease Investigator Group (PEDIG) studies emphasize that observation for 6 months is appropriate for isolated, non-traumatic 4th and 6th nerve palsies, as high rates of spontaneous recovery (up to 70-80%) are documented in microvascular cases.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Anesthesia Dolorosa (post-nerve injury).
Slipped or Lost Muscle (Surgical emergency).
Fat Adherence Syndrome (Common after repeated restrictive strabismus surgeries).
Prognosis: Restrictive cases are often stable but difficult to cure; Paralytic cases vary by etiology (vascular = good, traumatic = guarded).
